extraction.name: Prompted Textures Dataset (PTD)
extraction.description: Texture data serves as a valuable tool for interpreting the high-level features models learn, uncovering biases, and identifying security vulnerabilities. However, works in this space have been limited by small texture datasets and synthesis methods that struggle to scale in the diversity and specificity required for these tasks. In this work, we introduce an extensible methodology for generating high-quality, diverse texture images, which we use to create the Prompted Textures Dataset (PTD), a new texture dataset spanning 246,285 images across 56 texture classes. Our comparison against real texture data demonstrates that PTD is more diverse while maintaining quality. Additionally, human evaluations confirm that every stage in our methodology enhances texture quality, yielding a 3.4% increase in quality and a 4.5% increase in representativeness overall.
extraction.creator: Blaine Hoak, Patrick McDaniel
extraction.rai:dataCollection: We introduce an extensible methodology for generating high-quality, diverse texture images. Our approach takes place in three steps. First, we produce texture-specific prompts to serve as the basis for our texture generation, where we apply combinations of artistically-informed descriptors across a wide range of texture classes to enable controlled diversity of textures. Second, we use our constructed prompts as inputs to Stable Diffusion model pipelines, which we adapt based on unique challenges we uncover that arise from safety filters sensitivity to texture data, to produce the corresponding texture images. Finally, to yield higher-quality and more texture-like images, we perform a three stage refinement process consisting of frequency analysis, patch variance filtering, and CLIP scoring to filter down the images.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: A notable challenge during image generation was achieving images that passed the NSFW filter, despite using benign prompts. This filtering process replaces flagged images with black screens. This filtering issue proved substantial, with up to 60% of our initial generated images being flagged as NSFW. While we found no explicit content in flagged images, we excluded these images from further analysis for ethical reasons and did not release them publicly. After generating 5 (not flagged) images per prompt, we had a total of 483,840 images before additional refinement.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of images generated from texture-specific prompts using the Stable Diffusion model. Descriptive prompts are translated into visually representative texture images by adapting traditional text-to-image pipelines with texture-specific considerations.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Prompts were created by selecting descriptors from 56 texture classes (47 from Describable Textures Dataset and 9 new ones) and additional descriptive categories (artistic, spatial, enhancer, color) inspired by the 7 basic elements of art. Prompts were structured by combining one word from each category in standard English adjective order: {Artistic} {Spatial} {Color Enhancer} {Color} {Texture}. This resulted in 96,768 unique prompts for generating texture images.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A multi-stage refinement process was applied to ensure high quality, diversity, and alignment with prompts. This process consisted of three filtering steps: (1) frequency filtering to remove object-like images (retaining the top 80% of images with the highest frequency cutoff values), (2) patch variance filtering to eliminate homogeneous images (filtering out the bottom 20% of images with the lowest mean patch variance), and (3) CLIP score filtering to ensure alignment with the prompts (filtering out the bottom 20% of images with the lowest CLIP scores). After these stages, the dataset contained 246,285 images.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset images are associated with descriptive text prompts that were constructed to guide their generation. Additionally, a human evaluation was conducted where 9 participants rated 900 unique images. For each image, participants were asked two questions: (1) How would you rate the overall quality of the image? and (2) How well does the image represent the provided descriptor? Ratings were on a scale of 1 to 5, with 1 being the worst and 5 being the best.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human evaluation results were analyzed by taking the mean quality and representativeness scores across images at different stages of the refinement process. It was observed that each refinement step (frequency filtering, patch variance filtering, CLIP filtering) gradually improved both quality and representativeness. Combining all refinement steps resulted in an overall 3.4% increase in quality and a 4.5% increase in representativeness. Patch Variance and CLIP refinement contributed most to the increases. Quality trends across prompts were also analyzed using human representative scores, prompt-specific commentary, and CLIP scores, finding that some word pairs are more compatible than others and influence image quality.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For the human evaluation, 9 participants each provided 1 rating for overall quality and 1 rating for representativeness per image, for a total of 9 ratings for quality and 9 ratings for representativeness per image.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: CLIP scores were used for filtering images in the refinement process to ensure alignment with descriptive prompts. CLIP scores measure cosine similarity between image and text embeddings from a pre-trained CLIP model.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The Prompted Textures Dataset serves as a valuable tool for interpreting high-level features models learn, uncovering biases, and identifying security vulnerabilities. It contributes to advancing interpretability, bias analysis, and robustness in machine learning. The dataset has been used to develop new texture bias measurement methodologies, such as Texture Object Association Values (TAV), which helps understand how texture type affects model accuracy and confidence, and its impact on model trustworthiness.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: A significant challenge was the Stable Diffusion model's content safety filter, which flagged up to 60% of initial generated images as NSFW, despite using benign prompts. Texture descriptors like 'paisley' consistently triggered the filter. These flagged images were excluded from the final dataset for ethical reasons, highlighting the need for refined NSFW filters that can better handle abstract or texture-based content, and indicating a bias in the filtering process that affected the dataset's composition.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: There is room for improvement in generating more structured textures, as certain textures like 'grid' and 'polka-dotted' tended to have worse Inception and FID scores compared to more complex textures like 'hairy' and 'flaky'. The NSFW filtering issue also represents a limitation in the generation process, as it led to the exclusion of a large portion of initially generated images.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for understanding the high-level features models learn, uncovering biases, identifying security vulnerabilities, and conducting large-scale texture analysis. It is particularly useful for measuring texture bias in object classification models, studying texture-object associations, and advancing interpretability, bias analysis, and robustness in machine learning.
